section.title: Let Everything Praise the Lord
section.sectionRationale: The Psalter's final Hallelujah psalm and its crescendo, naming where, why, and how to praise before summoning every living, breathing creature to join the chorus, the fitting climax of a book that moves from lament to unbroken praise, and the goal of all things fulfilled when every creature in heaven and on earth praises God and the Lamb, Revelation 5:13.
section.thesis: The whole Psalter climbs toward this final command, let everything that has breath praise the LORD, a summons fulfilled when all creation joins in unending praise to God and the Lamb.
section.frameNote: Three movements: where and why to praise, verses 1-2; how to praise, with a full orchestra of instruments, verses 3-5; and who is summoned to praise, everything that has breath, verse 6.

verses.text: {{haleluyah|Hallelujah}}! Praise God in His sanctuary. Praise Him in His mighty heavens.
Praise Him for His mighty acts; praise Him for His excellent greatness.

units.label: Praise Him with the sound of the horn
units.note: how to praise, a full orchestra of worship

verses.text: Praise Him with the sound of the horn; praise Him with the harp and lyre.
Praise Him with tambourine and dancing; praise Him with strings and flute.
Praise Him with clashing cymbals; praise Him with resounding cymbals.

units.label: Let everything that has breath praise the Lord
units.note: who is called to praise, the goal of all things

verses.text: Let everything that has {{neshamah|breath}} praise the LORD! {{haleluyah|Hallelujah}}!

haleluyah.gloss: An imperative call, praise the LORD. It opens and closes each of the last five psalms and, here at the very end of the Psalter, brings the whole book's final movement of praise to its crescendo.

neshamah.gloss: Breath, or the breath of life, the same word for the breath God breathed into Adam, Genesis 2:7. Every living creature that breathes owes that breath to God and is summoned here to return it to Him in praise.

basic.context: This is the Psalter's final psalm, its crescendo, naming where praise belongs, in God's sanctuary and His mighty heavens, why it is due, His mighty acts and excellent greatness, and how it should sound, a full orchestra of instruments, before summoning every breathing creature to join.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a hymn of pure, unqualified praise, with no petition, no lament, and no condition attached. Its abiding pattern is that praise belongs to God everywhere, for everything He has done and is, expressed with every gift and voice available, by everyone who lives.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm opens and closes with haleluyah, and its final line summons everything that has neshamah, breath, to praise the LORD, the same breath God breathed into Adam at creation, now called to return to Him as praise.
basic.typology: The universal summons of verse 6, let everything that has breath praise the LORD, anticipates Revelation 5:13's vision of every creature in heaven and on earth, and under the earth and in the sea, singing praise and honor and glory to Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb.
basic.christ: This psalm's unqualified, universal praise finds its object completed in Christ. Revelation 5:13 shows every creature that has breath, exactly this psalm's summons, finally praising God and the Lamb together, the goal toward which the whole Psalter, and the whole story of redemption, has been moving.
basic.god: God is praised here simply for who He is and what He has done, His mighty acts and His excellent greatness, in the fullness of His dwelling place, both His earthly sanctuary and His mighty heavens, worthy of every instrument and every living voice.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 2:7 describes God breathing the breath of life into Adam, the same breath this psalm calls every creature to return to Him in praise. Revelation 5:13 pictures the fulfillment of this psalm's summons, every creature in heaven and on earth, and in the sea, praising God and the Lamb forever.
basic.oneStory: The Psalter began in the laments and struggles of Book I and climbs, psalm by psalm, toward this final, unbroken crescendo of praise, a summons completed when every creature that has breath, in the new creation, praises God and the Lamb together forever.

context.literary:
The shape of Psalm 150 is as plain as a drumbeat and just as deliberate. The Hebrew verb halal, to praise, is an imperative in every line of verses 1 to 5, and counting the opening and closing Hallelujah it sounds thirteen times in six verses. The psalm has no petition, no complaint, no title line naming an author or a tune, and it never pauses to tell a story. It simply asks three questions and answers each: where, why and how, and then, in the last verse, who.

The movement runs from the greatest scale to the smallest. Verse 1 begins in the sanctuary and the vault of the heavens, as high and wide as worship can reach. Verse 2 names the reasons. Verses 3 to 5 gather the players, moving through horn, strings, tambourine, flute and cymbals, so that wind, strings and percussion all have a place. Then verse 6 narrows from the heavens to a single breath in the nostrils of a living creature. The psalm starts at the top of the world and ends at the lips of the one who is singing.

It also stands at the end of a small group. Psalms 146 to 150 each open and close with Hallelujah, and they climb: Psalm 146 praises the LORD for His faithfulness to the oppressed, Psalm 147 for His care of Jerusalem and creation, Psalm 148 calls on the heavens and the earth to join, Psalm 149 gives Israel a new song, and Psalm 150 takes all of that and removes every limit. The Hebrew title of the whole book is Tehillim, Praises, from the same root, so the final psalm is the book's own name turned into a command.
context.historical:
The instruments in verses 3 to 5 are not an imaginary orchestra. They are the ones named in the story of Israel's worship. David told the Levite leaders to appoint singers to lift their voices with joy, accompanied by harps, lyres and cymbals, 1 Chronicles 15:16. At the dedication of Solomon's temple the Levitical singers stood by the altar with cymbals, harps and lyres, with a hundred and twenty priests sounding trumpets, and the temple filled with the cloud of the LORD's glory, 2 Chronicles 5:12-14. When Hezekiah restored the temple the song of the LORD began with the burnt offering, with the instruments of David, 2 Chronicles 29:25-28, and at the dedication of the rebuilt wall the Levites again came with cymbals, harps and lyres, Nehemiah 12:27.

The tambourine and dancing belong to an older and more popular joy. Miriam took a tambourine after the sea and all the women followed with tambourines and dancing, Exodus 15:20-21, and David and the whole house of Israel celebrated before the LORD with every kind of instrument when the ark came up, 2 Samuel 6:5. The horn is the shofar, sounded on the Day of Atonement in the year of Jubilee, Leviticus 25:9, and at the feasts, Psalm 81:3. So the psalm gathers the priestly, the royal and the festive music of Israel into one sound.

The psalm cannot be dated precisely, but the Psalter reached its final form after the exile, when Israel had known what it was to hang up its harps by the rivers of Babylon, Psalm 137:2-4. A people who had once asked how they could sing the LORD's song in a foreign land received, at the end of their songbook, the command to sing without reserve. The sanctuary in view is the temple at Jerusalem, rebuilt and in use, where God had set His name. Later Jewish morning prayer still gathers Psalms 145 to 150 as its closing chorus of praise.
context.canonical:
The Psalter is divided into five books, echoing the five books of Moses, and four of the five end with a short blessing: Psalm 41:13, Psalm 72:18-19, Psalm 89:52 and Psalm 106:48. Each is a verse or two of benediction, 'Amen and Amen.' Psalm 150 is the fifth, and it is not a verse added to a psalm but a whole psalm given to the doxology, as if the last book had so much to say that a verse was not enough. It also answers the book's opening. Psalm 1 begins with one blessed person who meditates on the law of the LORD, Psalm 1:1-2; Psalm 150 ends with every living creature joining in praise. The book that began with a single reader ends with a whole creation.

The call to praise also has its seeds in the psalms just before. Psalm 145 closes with 'let every creature bless His holy name forever and ever,' Psalm 145:21, and Psalm 148 had already summoned sun and moon, sea creatures, wild animals, kings and children, Psalm 148:3-12. Psalm 150 is the point where all those voices become one.

The New Testament picks the motif up and carries it forward. The word Hallelujah appears in the Greek New Testament only in Revelation 19, where a great multitude in heaven cries it four times, Revelation 19:1-6, and the whole creation in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea answers with praise to God and to the Lamb, Revelation 5:13. Paul tells believers to sing psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, Colossians 3:16 and Ephesians 5:19, and Hebrews urges 'a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name,' Hebrews 13:15. When some Pharisees tried to quiet the disciples' praise at the entry into Jerusalem, Jesus said that the very stones would cry out, Luke 19:37-40.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Whoever shaped the Psalter's ending wanted its readers to know where all the songs were going. The Psalter has taken in complaint, confession, history, wisdom and royal triumph, and it ends neither in an answer to every question nor in a final complaint, but in praise. The editors place this psalm last to teach that worship is not one department of life beside the others; it is the destination of them all. A reader who has come through the wilderness psalms is meant to arrive here with the conviction that God is worth praising even before the troubles are solved.

The psalm is also meant to enlarge the reader's imagination. It does not stop at the temple walls. By setting the sanctuary beside the heavens and ending with every breathing creature, it tells Israel that the praise they offer in Jerusalem is a small part of something that fills the universe.

Finally, it is an invitation, not a performance. The commands are in the plural and the last verse leaves no one out. The first hearers were meant to hear their own name in 'everything that has breath' and to answer.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is one of the clearest commands in Scripture, and it is a command to do something, not merely an account of what others did. Praise is the thing being prescribed. What the psalm gives as examples are the means, and those are drawn from the culture and the worship of ancient Israel: the horn, the harp, the tambourine, the clashing cymbals. The Bible elsewhere holds worship with reverence and awe, Hebrews 12:28, and also teaches silence before the LORD in His holy temple, Habakkuk 2:20, so no single volume or style is being legislated here.

What carries over is the pattern. Praise should be wholehearted, with body and voice and skill; it should have reasons, rooted in what God has done and who He is, verse 2; and it should be shared by a whole people. The Lord Jesus taught that true worshippers worship the Father in spirit and in truth, John 4:23-24, which means the heart is what the instruments serve. Nothing in the psalm turns the instruments into a ritual requirement, and nothing in it permits worship that is half asleep.

debates.question: What is 'His sanctuary' in verse 1, and how does it relate to 'His mighty heavens'?

views.label: The temple at Jerusalem, with the heavens as the wider sphere of praise
views.case: The musicians and instruments are those of the temple, 2 Chronicles 5:12-13, and the Psalter often speaks of the sanctuary as the place where God is praised in the assembly, Psalm 22:25. On this reading verse 1 moves from the building on earth to the vault of the sky over it, so that the whole world is the temple's courtyard.

views.label: The heavenly sanctuary, so that both lines describe one place above
views.case: The two lines are parallel and the second names the heavens. Psalm 11:4 sets the LORD in His holy temple and on His heavenly throne together, and Hebrews 9:24 speaks of heaven itself as the true sanctuary. On this reading the first hearers are summoned to join praise already going on above, including the praise of the angels, Psalm 148:2.

views.label: Both, with the earthly temple as an echo of the heavenly
views.case: Israel understood its sanctuary as a copy of a greater reality, and the psalm does not need to choose. The temple is where earth joins in; the heavens are the larger house in which the praise rises.

debates.bearing: The reading chosen changes little for the command and a good deal for the scale. On every view the psalm refuses to let praise be confined to a room: it begins where God dwells and it reaches the whole world by the last verse.

debates.question: Who is included in 'everything that has breath' in verse 6?

views.label: Every human being
views.case: The Hebrew word for breath, neshamah, is used of the breath God breathed into Adam, Genesis 2:7, and Isaiah 42:5 says He gives breath to the people on the earth. Job 33:4 speaks of the breath of the Almighty giving life to a person. The call is then to the whole human race, beyond Israel.

views.label: All living creatures, human and animal
views.case: Genesis 7:22 uses nearly the same phrase for everything on dry land that had the breath of life in its nostrils, which includes the animals. Psalm 148:10 calls wild animals and cattle, creeping things and flying birds to praise. On this view the psalm has a creaturely scope that reaches beyond people.

views.label: A summons to the whole creation, including what has no lungs
views.case: Psalm 148 also calls on sun, moon, stars and mountains, and Revelation 5:13 hears the sea and all that is in it give praise. Breath may be the psalm's picture of life itself, with the inanimate creation addressed by the neighbouring psalms.

debates.bearing: The first two readings are held together by the Old Testament's own usage, and the third by the neighbouring psalms. All agree that no part of the living world is outside the call, and that people, who can know why they praise, are asked to lead the rest.

debates.question: Does the list of instruments set a pattern for the church's worship today?

views.label: It describes Israel's practice and prescribes no particular instrument
views.case: The temple music of Chronicles was set up under David and his prophets, 2 Chronicles 29:25, and belonged to the ceremonies of that building. The New Testament speaks of psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, Ephesians 5:19, without listing instruments, and different cultures have different gifts to offer.

views.label: It prescribes a principle of whole hearted, skilful, embodied praise
views.case: Psalm 33:3 asks for skilful playing with a shout of joy, and the psalm's catalogue, with its dance and its clash of cymbals, models a worship that uses every gift. On this reading the church should bring what skill it has without embarrassment.

debates.bearing: The two readings agree that praise should be wholehearted. They differ on how far the specific forms bind, and the psalm's own spirit points to the heart in the instruments more than the instruments themselves.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb halal sits behind the whole psalm. In its piel form, the form of the repeated command here, it means to praise, to celebrate with the voice. The related reflexive form can mean to boast, as in Psalm 34:2, 'My soul boasts in the LORD,' and in Jeremiah 9:23-24, where the one who boasts is told to boast in knowing the LORD. That shade matters. Praise in Scripture is the opposite of boasting in oneself: it is the joyful turning of one's pride outward to God. The 'Hallelu' that begins the psalm is a plural command addressed to a congregation, and it joins Yah, the short form of the divine name. Verse 1 then speaks of praising God as El, and verse 6 closes with Yah again, so that the covenant name frames the whole.

The second line of verse 1 uses raqia, the word for the expanse that God made on the second day, Genesis 1:6-8, and the BSB footnote notes the alternative 'in the expanse of His might.' The line sets the vault of the sky beside the sanctuary as though it were another room of the house, a vault that proclaims His power.

A small syllable carries a good deal. The prefix be, meaning in, with or for, governs place in verse 1, the grounds for praise in the first line of verse 2, and the means in verses 3 to 5, 'with the blast of the horn,' 'with tambourine.' The second line of verse 2 changes to ke, 'according to,' as the measure: according to the abundance of His greatness. The word for greatness, gudlo, comes from the same root as the 'unsearchable' greatness of Psalm 145:3, which means praise is asked to match something with no measure. The 'mighty acts' of verse 2 are gevurot, plural and concrete, the deeds the generations are to proclaim in Psalm 145:4.

The instruments have their own stories. The word for horn is shofar, the ram's horn of the Jubilee, Leviticus 25:9. The harp and the lyre, nevel and kinnor, and the flute, ugav, appear together in Genesis 4:21, where Jubal is the father of those who play them, and in Job 21:12, where the prosperous wicked play them without any thought of God. The psalm takes the same instruments and points them to the LORD. The word for dancing, machol, is joined to the tambourine as in Psalm 149:3 and Psalm 30:11, though some have taken it as a pipe. The two kinds of cymbals are named differently, one of hearing and one of teru'ah, the word for a shout or blast of acclamation, as in Psalm 33:3 and Psalm 89:15, so the second kind is a cymbal of joyful cry.

Finally the neshamah of verse 6 is not any breath but the word used for the breath God breathed into Adam, Genesis 2:7, and Job 33:4 calls it the breath of the Almighty. The verb, tehallel, is singular: all the breathing creatures become one voice. The Greek Old Testament leaves Hallelujah untranslated, as Revelation 19 later does, and gives verse 6 as every breath, using its ordinary word for breath.

typology.type: The temple orchestra in the sanctuary, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: Praise in Psalm 150 is set in God's sanctuary, and the sanctuary was the place where heaven and earth met in Israel's life, with the Levites playing before the cloud of glory, 2 Chronicles 5:12-14. In Christ the place of meeting becomes a person. Jesus called the temple of His body the temple that would be raised, John 2:19-21, and Hebrews says He entered heaven itself, the true sanctuary, Hebrews 9:24. Believers are now being built together into a dwelling for God in the Spirit, Ephesians 2:21-22. The type falls short in that the old sanctuary needed to be visited; the new one goes with the people of God, so praise is no longer bound to one address.

typology.type: Miriam's tambourine and the dancing, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: Tambourine and dancing first appear in Israel's worship on the far shore of the sea, when Miriam and the women sang about the horse and rider thrown into the sea, Exodus 15:20-21. John sees the same scene lifted to heaven, with the victors standing by a sea of glass holding harps from God and singing the song of Moses and of the Lamb, Revelation 15:2-4. The deliverance from Egypt is the pattern, and the Lamb's victory is the fulfilment, with all nations coming to worship. The type is limited in that Miriam's song rejoiced in an enemy's defeat for one people, while the new song celebrates a rescue bought for people from every tribe and tongue, Revelation 5:9.

The breath God breathed into the first man, Genesis 2:7, is what the psalm calls to praise. That first breath failed to hold off death, and Psalm 104:29 says that when God takes it away they die. The risen Jesus breathes on His disciples and says 'Receive the Holy Spirit,' John 20:22, a deliberate echo of the first creation. The escalation is that this breath gives life that death cannot take back, and the Spirit sent in this new creation fills believers so that they speak to one another in psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, Ephesians 5:18-19. Still the type is partial: believers have the first fruits of the Spirit and still groan, Romans 8:23, awaiting the full redemption.

typology.type: The Levitical musicians and the royal priesthood, verses 3 to 5
typology.fulfillment: Only the Levites were appointed to lift their voices with instruments before the LORD, 1 Chronicles 15:16, as a class set apart. The New Testament widens the circle. Peter calls the church a royal priesthood to proclaim the virtues of Him who called them from darkness into light, 1 Peter 2:9, and the elders in heaven sing that the Lamb has made people from every nation a kingdom and priests, Revelation 5:9-10. Hebrews tells all believers, through Jesus, to offer 'a sacrifice of praise,' Hebrews 13:15. What a tribe once did on behalf of Israel, the whole people now does together. The correspondence is real, but the shadow is surpassed: no human mediator stands before the singers, because Jesus is the great priest over the house of God, Hebrews 10:21.

study.christ:
Psalm 150 is not a prophecy about the Messiah, and it is wiser to say so than to force one. It leads to Christ the way the end of a long road leads to its destination: by showing what the whole Psalter has been aiming at, and by telling us who at last makes that aim possible.

First, Christ is the leader of the praise. Hebrews takes the vow of Psalm 22:22, 'I will proclaim Your name to My brothers; I will sing Your praises in the assembly,' and puts it in the mouth of Jesus, Hebrews 2:12. The one who sang a hymn with His disciples on the night He was betrayed, Matthew 26:30, is the singer in the midst of the congregation. When the whole multitude of disciples praised God joyfully for all the miracles they had seen at the entry into Jerusalem, and the Pharisees demanded silence, He said that if they were silent the stones would cry out, Luke 19:37-40. Worship has a Leader before it has a choir.

Second, Christ is the reason for the 'mighty acts' of verse 2. The song of Revelation 5 gives the content: 'Worthy is the Lamb, who was slain,' Revelation 5:12. The greatest of God's deeds in praise is the cross and the empty tomb, and the heavens are not silent about them. Philippians 2:9-11 says that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. The summons to everything that has breath is answered there.

Third, Christ is the Creator and sustainer whose breath the creatures borrow. Colossians says that all things were created through Him and for Him and that in Him they hold together, Colossians 1:16-17. The breath that Psalm 150 summons was given by the One it is summoned to praise, and the risen Lord breathes the Spirit on His people, John 20:22.

Fourth, Christ is the sanctuary and the way into it. His body is the temple, John 2:19-21, and through the curtain of His body believers enter the Most Holy Place, Hebrews 10:19-20. The place where praise is offered is no longer a building to be reached but a person to be known.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The harp and the cymbals are not secret symbols of Jesus, and the psalm's thirteen praises do not stand for His names. The link is built from what the New Testament does with the praise this psalm commands: it makes Christ its leader, its ground and its goal.
study.god:
The psalm shows a God who is both high above the world and close enough to be praised in a building. He is to be praised in His sanctuary and in His mighty heavens, the same God, one in both places. Psalm 11:4 holds the pair together, the LORD in His holy temple and on His heavenly throne, and Isaiah's vision of the seraphim shows the earth already full of the glory heaven proclaims, Isaiah 6:1-3. The God of Psalm 150 is transcendent without being remote.

The two reasons in verse 2, His mighty acts and His excellent greatness, name two sides of what praise answers to: what He does and what He is. His acts are the visible record, creation and rescue and judgment, the things generations pass on to one another, Psalm 145:4. His greatness is the unsearchable fullness behind the acts, Psalm 145:3. A God known only by His acts might be thought to be as good as His last favour; a God known only by His greatness might seem far off. The psalm holds both, and so praise can continue when the favours seem few.

It shows God as the source of breath. Every creature that is told to praise has breath because He gave it, Isaiah 42:5, and Psalm 104:29-30 describes Him taking breath away and sending His Spirit to renew the face of the earth. This means praise is not a favour offered to a needy God. Paul says God is not served by human hands as if He needed anything, because He gives everyone life and breath, Acts 17:25. The creature praises because it owes everything, and because praise is what it is made for, Isaiah 43:21.

Still, the God of this psalm is no cold, self-sufficient monarch indifferent to His people's voices. Psalm 22:3 says He is enthroned on the praises of Israel, and the temple stories show Him filling the house with glory when the singers join as one voice, 2 Chronicles 5:13-14. He is a God who delights to be praised and who is not diminished by the noise of cymbals and tambourines.

He is also the God for whom the joy must not displace honesty. Psalm 51:16-17 says that the sacrifices He wants are a broken spirit, and Psalm 150 does not contradict that. The Psalter has let every lament and confession be heard before it lets this crescendo sound, so the praise is not shallow.

For worship, the psalm teaches that praise belongs to the whole of life and the whole of the person, and that the object of praise is God Himself, not the music. It asks nothing less than all, and it assumes that the God who is worthy of everything is also gracious enough to receive it.

crossReferences.note: The breath of life that God breathed into the man, from which Psalm 150:6 takes its word for breath. Praise is thus the creature giving back what the Creator first gave, and the psalm's final summons has creation itself in view.

The neighbouring psalm that calls on angels, sun and moon, the deep, wild animals and cattle, kings and children to praise. Psalm 148 fills in the whole cast that Psalm 150:6 sweeps up in 'everything that has breath,' and it gives the same reason, that He alone is exalted.

The last verse before the Hallelujah psalms, 'let every creature bless His holy name forever and ever.' It sets out the destination the final five psalms then march toward, and Psalm 150:6 is its answer in the first person plural.

At the dedication of the temple the singers, trumpets, cymbals, harps and lyres sounded as one voice, and the house filled with the cloud of the LORD's glory. This is the scene the psalm's instruments recall, and it shows that God answers praise with His presence.

Miriam and the women with tambourines and dancing, singing to the LORD after the sea. The tambourine and dance of verse 4 first sound here, which ties the psalm's music to the great act of rescue from Egypt.

Praise the LORD with the harp, with the ten strings, with a new song, and play skilfully with a shout of joy. It shows the same spirit as verses 3 to 5, with the added call to skill, so enthusiasm and craftsmanship belong together.

God takes away breath and sends His Spirit, and the singer vows to sing all his life, ending with Hallelujah. It explains why the creature's breath is the right instrument of praise, and why the psalm calls it back to Him.

God the LORD, who created the heavens, spread out the earth and gives breath to the people on it. It names the Giver of the neshamah of verse 6 and shows that the whole human race, not Israel alone, lives on His gift.

When the disciples praised God in a loud voice at the entry into Jerusalem, Jesus said the stones would cry out if they were silent. It shows praise as so fitting to the moment that creation itself will fill the gap.

Through Jesus, believers continually offer a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name. It carries the psalm into the new covenant: the priest's offering becomes the voice of every believer, through the one mediator.
Every knee bows and every tongue confesses in heaven, on earth and under the earth that Jesus Christ is Lord. The cosmic scope of Psalm 150:6 appears here with its object named.

The only place the New Testament uses the word Hallelujah, shouted by the multitude in heaven four times as God reigns. Psalm 150 sets the pattern, and Revelation 19 is its fulfilment in the roar of many waters and thunder.

study.oneStory:
Praise was in the world before the psalm and before the people who sing it. When God laid the earth's foundations the morning stars sang together and the sons of God shouted for joy, Job 38:7, so the first chorus was heard before there was anyone to join it. Then God breathed into dust and a man became a living being, Genesis 2:7, and humanity was given a throat for the song. That is where Psalm 150 begins, with breath meant to be spent on praise.

The fall turned breath into a countdown. Death entered, and Psalm 104:29 shows what that means for every creature: God takes it away and they return to dust. Praise did not stop, but it became a thing of exceptions, sung by a rescued people on the far side of the sea, Exodus 15, in a temple with cymbals and cloud, 2 Chronicles 5, and finally in tears by the waters of Babylon where the harps hung silent on the willows, Psalm 137:1-4. The Psalter, edited after that exile, finishes where the exiles longed to be: singing without reserve.

But Psalm 150 is a command still waiting for its full answer. Creation has been subjected to futility and groans together as in childbirth, Romans 8:20-22, and the nations do not yet praise the LORD with one voice. The story moves toward the day it does. The Gospels put the firstfruits in the mouths of children in the temple, Matthew 21:15-16, and in the disciples on the road down from the Mount of Olives. Jesus Himself leads, Hebrews 2:12, and His resurrection breath is the pledge that the Spirit of the new creation is already moving, John 20:22.

Revelation lets us hear the end. First the angels and living creatures and elders sing worthy is the Lamb, and then every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea answers, Revelation 5:11-13. Then the great multitude shouts Hallelujah, and the sound is like many waters and thunder, Revelation 19:1-6. At the close of the Bible there is a city where God dwells with His people, there is no more curse, and His servants worship Him, Revelation 21:3 and Revelation 22:3. The breath that began in a garden ends in a city, and no one is silent.

quiz.q: Where does this psalm call for God to be praised, verse 1?

options.text: In His sanctuary and in His mighty heavens.
options.note: The psalm names both the earthly place of worship and the vast heavens as fitting places for praise.

options.text: Only in the wilderness, away from other people.
options.note: The psalm names the sanctuary and the heavens, not isolated wilderness.

options.text: Only in private, never in public gathering.
options.note: The sanctuary points to corporate, gathered worship, not only private devotion.

options.text: Primarily in the heavens, with the sanctuary as an afterthought.
options.note: Both locations are named together with equal weight in verse 1.

quiz.q: Why should God be praised, according to verse 2?

options.text: For His mighty acts and His excellent greatness.
options.note: The psalm grounds praise in both what God has done and who He is.

options.text: Only because it is a religious duty with no real reason.
options.note: The psalm gives specific, substantive reasons, His acts and His greatness.

options.text: Because He needs human praise to be complete.
options.note: The psalm presents praise as a fitting response to God, not a divine need.

options.text: For His mighty acts alone, with no mention of His character.
options.note: The verse names both His acts and His excellent greatness, His character.

quiz.q: How many kinds of instruments are named in verses 3-5?

options.text: Several, horn, harp, lyre, tambourine, strings, flute, and cymbals, a full orchestra of praise.
options.note: The psalm lists a wide and varied range of instruments and dancing.

options.text: Only one, the harp.
options.note: The list is deliberately extensive, not limited to a single instrument.

options.text: None; instruments are forbidden in worship.
options.note: The opposite is true; the psalm actively summons a wide range of instruments.

options.text: Only percussion instruments are named.
options.note: Strings, wind, and percussion instruments are all named together.

quiz.q: Who is called to praise the LORD in verse 6, the psalm's final line?

options.text: Everything that has breath.
options.note: The psalm's closing summons is deliberately universal, excluding no living creature.

options.text: Only the priests of Israel.
options.note: The summons is universal, not restricted to a priestly class.

options.text: Only the angels in heaven.
options.note: The phrase everything that has breath points to earthly, living creatures as well as heavenly beings.

options.text: Only the psalmist himself.
options.note: The final line widens far beyond the psalmist to every breathing creature.

quiz.q: How does Revelation 5:13 relate to this psalm's final summons?

options.text: It pictures the fulfillment, every creature in heaven and on earth, and in the sea, praising Him who sits on the throne and the Lamb forever.
options.note: Revelation 5:13 completes this psalm's universal call with a vision of its final, eternal fulfillment.

options.text: Revelation 5:13 contradicts this psalm's universal call to praise.
options.note: Revelation 5:13 fulfills, rather than contradicts, this psalm's summons.

options.text: The connection is only coincidental wording, with no theological significance.
options.note: The parallel is a deliberate, theologically significant fulfillment, not mere coincidence.

options.text: Revelation 5:13 limits the praise to angels alone, unlike this psalm.
options.note: Revelation 5:13 actually widens the praise further, to every creature, matching this psalm's own universal scope.

questions: This final psalm gives no reason to withhold praise, only reasons to give it. What is keeping you from wholehearted praise to God today?
The psalm calls for praise for His mighty acts and His excellent greatness, verse 2, both what God has done and who He is. Which is easier for you to praise Him for right now, and why?
A full orchestra of instruments is named, verses 3-5. What is your own instrument, your voice, your work, your art, that you can offer in praise this week?
Let everything that has breath praise the LORD includes you, in whatever you are facing today. What would it look like to let your very next breath be an act of praise?
The whole Psalter ends here, in unbroken praise, after so many psalms of lament. How does knowing this is where your own story ends, in praise, change how you carry a current sorrow?

translationNotes.note: His mighty heavens can also be rendered the expanse of His might, or the firmament of His might, echoing the same word used for the sky in Genesis 1:6-8.
Horn renders shofar, a ram's horn trumpet used in worship and as a call to assembly, distinct from the qeren, horn, image of Psalm 148:14.
Breath renders neshamah, the same word for the breath of life God breathed into Adam, Genesis 2:7, tying the psalm's final summons to every living creature.
